methodology: Stratified random sample by heuristic match score (5 = leaf+type-name match, e.g. issue_number/Issue.number; 4 = exact leaf-name match, non-generic). Each entry needs 'verdict' filled in by hand: 'correct' (the producer really does supply this value), 'incorrect' (coincidental/wrong match), or 'ambiguous' (genuinely unclear without deeper GitHub API knowledge). See eval/README.md.

entries.label: release_id

producer.description: Creates a release in a GitHub repository for a specified tag; the tag must be unique for published releases, and if a `discussion_category_name` is given, it must already exist.

consumer.description: Lists all reactions, or optionally filters reactions by a specific content type, for a given GitHub release.

entries.notes: release_id is assigned by GitHub upon creation, genuinely new info; producer does not require release_id itself.

entries.label: repository_id

producer.description: Creates a GitHub Codespace for the authenticated user, requiring a JSON request body with either `repository_id` (integer) or a `pull_request` object (containing `pull_request_number` (integer) and `repository_id` (integer)). This action allows users to set up a development environment quickly by creating a codespace from a specified repository or pull request.

consumer.description: Adds a repository to a GitHub App installation, granting the app access; requires authenticated user to have admin rights for the repository and access to the installation.

entries.notes: Catalog schema omits required entirely for this tool (a real gap: description says it needs repository_id or a pull_request object, but this OR-relationship is not encoded in a flat required array, so the circularity check cannot catch it). Practically, repository_id must be known to create the codespace in the first place -- the response just echoes it back.

entries.label: card_id

producer.description: Lists all project cards for a given column_id in GitHub Projects (classic). DEPRECATION NOTICE: GitHub Projects (classic) and its REST API were sunset on April 1, 2025. This action will return 404 for most requests on GitHub.com. However, it may still work on GitHub Enterprise Server instances where classic projects are enabled. For new projects, use GitHub Projects V2 which uses the GraphQL API instead. See: https://github.blog/changelog/2024-05-23-sunset-notice-projects-classic/ Returns a list of project cards including: id, node_id, url, note (or null for linked cards), creator info, content_url (for issue/PR cards), column_url, project_url, timestamps, and archived status.

consumer.description: Retrieves all details of a specific project card, given its unique `card_id`. DEPRECATION NOTICE: GitHub Projects (classic) REST API was sunset on April 1, 2025. This action only works with existing classic project cards that were created before the sunset date. For new projects, use GitHub Projects V2 (GraphQL API) instead.

entries.notes: Listing cards in a column requires only column_id, not card_id -- genuine discovery of card IDs. (Both tools are deprecated/sunset per GitHub, which is a real-world staleness concern but does not affect whether the matching logic itself is sound.)

entries.label: package_name

producer.description: Tool to retrieve a repository security advisory using its GHSA identifier. Use when you need detailed information about a specific security vulnerability.

consumer.description: Retrieves detailed information for an existing specific package version associated with the authenticated user, identified by its type, name, and version ID.

entries.notes: VulnerabilityPackage.name describes a third-party dependency named in a security advisory (e.g. "lodash"), which is a different thing from a package the AUTHENTICATED USER personally owns/publishes. Same string type, unrelated semantic context.

entries.label: project_number

producer.description: Creates a new GitHub Projects V2 project board linked to a specified repository. Note: This action uses GitHub's Projects V2 GraphQL API. The legacy Projects V1 REST API has been sunset by GitHub. The project is owned by the repository owner (user or organization) and linked to the specified repository.

consumer.description: Tool to add a custom field to a user-owned GitHub Projects V2 project. Use when you need to add fields like status, priority, or custom data to organize project items.

entries.notes: project_number is assigned on creation, genuinely new. The project is owned by "the repository owner (user or organization)" per its description -- when the owner is a user account, this is a legitimate user-owned project_number.

entries.label: package_version_id

producer.description: Lists all versions of a public package owned by a specific GitHub user, identified by package type, package name, and username.

consumer.description: Restores a specific, user-owned package version if it was deleted within the last 30 days and its original namespace and version name are still available.

entries.notes: Both tools operate on packages owned by the same user; package_version_id is discovered via listing, not required to list.

entries.label: environment_name

producer.description: Retrieves pending deployment environments for a specific workflow run that are awaiting approval due to protection rules.

consumer.description: Retrieves a specific custom deployment protection rule (used by GitHub Apps for external validation or manual approval of deployments) for a given environment in a repository.

entries.notes: Pending deployments genuinely reveal which environment(s) are awaiting approval -- you would not know environment_name without checking this first.

entries.label: user_id

producer.description: Adds a GitHub user as a repository collaborator, or updates their permission if already a collaborator; `permission` applies to organization-owned repositories (personal ones default to 'push' and ignore this field), and an invitation may be created or permissions updated directly.

consumer.description: Tool to unfollow a GitHub user using GraphQL. Use when you need to stop following a specific user on GitHub.

entries.notes: Producer requires only username (not user_id) to add a collaborator; the invitee.id in the response is a genuine username-to-numeric-id lookup, useful for the GraphQL consumer that needs the numeric id.

entries.label: secret_name

producer.description: Lists GitHub Actions secrets available for a specified organization.

consumer.description: Creates or updates an organization's GitHub Codespaces secret using an encrypted value and its corresponding public key ID.

entries.notes: Listing org secrets requires only org; secret_name is discovered from the list, not required to produce it.

entries.label: run_id

producer.description: Creates a new check run for a specific commit in a repository, used by external services to report status, detailed feedback, annotations, and images directly within the GitHub UI. NOTE: This endpoint requires GitHub App authentication - OAuth tokens and personal access tokens cannot create check runs.

consumer.description: Lists jobs for a specific workflow run in a GitHub repository.

entries.notes: A check run id (a single CI check, e.g. "lint") is a different resource from a workflow run id (an entire workflow execution containing multiple jobs) in the real GitHub API. The match happened because CreateACheckRunResponse tokenizes to include "run" (from "Check Run"), which coincidentally satisfies the type-name-agreement rule for the unrelated concept "run_id". A genuinely new heuristic limitation: type names sharing a word ("run") across different resources.

entries.label: pull_number

producer.description: Converts an open pull request to draft status, indicating it is not ready for review. Use this action when you need to mark a PR as work-in-progress after it has been opened. Draft pull requests cannot be merged until they are marked as ready for review. This action is useful when additional work is needed before the PR can be reviewed or merged.

consumer.description: Gets all users and teams requested to review a specific pull request in a repository.

entries.notes: Producer requires pullRequestId (a GraphQL node ID), a different identifier space from pull_number (the numeric PR number) -- the response genuinely supplies new, useful information: the human-readable number for a PR you only had the GraphQL ID for.

entries.label: event_id

producer.description: Lists public events for the specified GitHub user, or private events if authenticated as that user, in reverse chronological order.

consumer.description: Fetches details of a specific issue event for a given repository and event ID.

entries.notes: A user's general public activity feed event (GitHub Events API: PushEvent, WatchEvent, etc.) is a different resource from an issue timeline event (Issue Events API: labeled, assigned, etc.) -- unrelated endpoints that both happen to be casually called "events" with an "id" field.

entries.label: milestone_number

producer.description: Closes an open pull request without merging it. The pull request state is set to "closed" and it can be reopened later if needed. Use this action when you want to reject or abandon a pull request without merging the proposed changes into the base branch. You must have write access to the repository to close pull requests.

consumer.description: Updates a milestone in a repository, identified by `owner`, `repo`, and `milestone_number`, by allowing modification of its `title`, `state`, `description`, or `due_on`; at least one of these four attributes must be provided to perform an update.

entries.notes: A pull request can have an associated milestone; closing it can reveal that milestone (including its number) if one was assigned, without having needed to know milestone_number beforehand. Conditional on a milestone actually being assigned, but a genuine, non-circular relationship when it is.

entries.label: team_slug

producer.description: Creates a pull request in a GitHub repository, requiring existing `base` and `head` branches; `title` or `issue` must be provided.

consumer.description: Deletes a specific comment from an existing team discussion within an organization, provided the specified organization, team, discussion, and comment all exist.

entries.notes: Even setting aside that requested_teams reflects teams you would have specified yourself when creating the PR, there is no reason the specific team requested for PR review is the team relevant to an unrelated, arbitrary team-discussion comment deletion. Coincidental field-name/type match across unrelated workflows.

entries.label: project_number

producer.description: Creates a new classic project board within a specified GitHub organization. Note: This action uses GitHub's Projects (classic) REST API. The classic projects feature may be disabled in some organizations, and GitHub recommends migrating to Projects V2 (accessible via GraphQL API) for new projects. Requirements: - The authenticated user must be an organization member with project creation permissions - Classic projects must be enabled for the organization - Requires 'repo' and 'admin:org' or 'write:org' scopes

consumer.description: Tool to delete a project item for a user in GitHub Projects V2. Use when you need to remove an item from a user's project. Requires the project item's GraphQL node ID (starts with 'PVTI_'). Uses the GitHub GraphQL API deleteProjectV2Item mutation.

entries.notes: GitHub Projects V2 numbers are scoped per-owner: an organization-owned project's project_number is a different, independently-numbered sequence from a user-owned project's project_number. Producer is explicitly organization-scoped; consumer is explicitly _FOR_USER -- a real namespace mismatch, not the same identifier space.

entries.label: issue_number

producer.description: Creates a new issue in a GitHub repository, requiring the repository to exist and have issues enabled; specific fields like assignees, milestone, or labels may require push access.

consumer.description: Close a GitHub issue by setting its state to closed. Use this action when you need to mark an issue as resolved or no longer relevant. Optionally specify a reason for closing (completed or not_planned) to provide context.

entries.notes: issue_number is assigned by GitHub upon creation, genuinely new info; producer does not require issue_number itself.

entries.label: run_id

producer.description: Gets a specific artifact for a repository by `artifact_id`. This action retrieves the details of a specific artifact from a GitHub repository using the artifact's unique identifier. It allows users to access information about artifacts stored in the repository.

consumer.description: Approves a workflow run from a forked repository's pull request; call this when such a run requires manual approval due to workflow configuration.

entries.notes: Artifact details genuinely include the id of the workflow_run that produced them (WorkflowRunInfo.id) -- a real, exact relationship, unlike the coincidental token-collision cases.

entries.label: column_id

producer.description: Lists all of a GitHub project's columns (e.g., 'To Do', 'In Progress'); project_id must identify a valid, accessible project. Note: This action uses GitHub's Projects (classic) REST API. The Projects (classic) API was sunset on April 1, 2025. This action will return an empty columns list with an informative message for projects that no longer exist or when the API returns 404.

consumer.description: Moves a column within a GitHub project (classic) to a new position. DEPRECATION NOTICE: GitHub Classic Projects (V1) and its REST API were sunset on April 1, 2025. This action will return a 404 error on GitHub.com. For new projects, use GitHub Projects V2 which uses the GraphQL API instead. The `position` parameter can be: - 'first': Move the column to the beginning of the project - 'last': Move the column to the end of the project - 'after:<column_id>': Place the column after the specified column (e.g., 'after:67890') See: https://github.blog/changelog/2024-05-23-sunset-notice-projects-classic/

entries.notes: Listing columns requires only project_id, not column_id -- genuine discovery.

entries.label: column_id

producer.description: Lists all of a GitHub project's columns (e.g., 'To Do', 'In Progress'); project_id must identify a valid, accessible project. Note: This action uses GitHub's Projects (classic) REST API. The Projects (classic) API was sunset on April 1, 2025. This action will return an empty columns list with an informative message for projects that no longer exist or when the API returns 404.

consumer.description: Lists all project cards for a given column_id in GitHub Projects (classic). DEPRECATION NOTICE: GitHub Projects (classic) and its REST API were sunset on April 1, 2025. This action will return 404 for most requests on GitHub.com. However, it may still work on GitHub Enterprise Server instances where classic projects are enabled. For new projects, use GitHub Projects V2 which uses the GraphQL API instead. See: https://github.blog/changelog/2024-05-23-sunset-notice-projects-classic/ Returns a list of project cards including: id, node_id, url, note (or null for linked cards), creator info, content_url (for issue/PR cards), column_url, project_url, timestamps, and archived status.

entries.notes: Same relationship as #17.

entries.label: comment_id

producer.description: Creates a comment on a specific commit, or on a specific line if `path` and `position` are provided.

consumer.description: Retrieves a specific Gist comment by its ID and the Gist's ID.

entries.notes: A commit comment id and a gist comment id are different, independently-numbered resources in the real GitHub API -- a commit-comment ID has no meaning as a gist comment ID. Consumer also requires gist_id, which the producer has no way to supply at all (no gist is involved in commenting on a commit).

entries.label: comment_id

producer.description: Creates a comment on a specific commit, or on a specific line if `path` and `position` are provided.

consumer.description: Creates a reaction for a specific comment on an issue within a GitHub repository.

entries.notes: A commit comment id and an issue comment id are different, independently-numbered resources -- same class of mistake as #19, just a different target resource.

entries.label: gist_id

producer.description: Lists gists for the authenticated user, with optional filtering by update time and pagination.

consumer.description: Deletes a specific comment from a GitHub Gist using its `gist_id` and `comment_id`.

entries.notes: Listing your own gists requires nothing; gist_id is genuinely discovered from the list.

entries.label: secret_name

producer.description: Lists all Codespaces secrets available for a specified organization, which must exist.

consumer.description: Revokes a specific repository's access to an organization-level Dependabot secret, applicable only when the secret has 'selected' visibility and the specified repository currently has access.

entries.notes: Producer lists Codespaces secrets; consumer (per its own description) operates on an organization-level Dependabot secret. Codespaces and Dependabot secrets are separate, independently-namespaced secret stores in GitHub -- a name from one does not carry over to the other even if the literal string happens to match.

entries.label: secret_name

producer.description: Lists GitHub Actions secrets available for a specified organization.

consumer.description: Adds a repository to an organization secret's access list when the secret's visibility is 'selected'; this operation is idempotent.

entries.notes: Both concern the same kind of organization (Actions) secret; no category mismatch signal here unlike #22/#26.

entries.label: repository_id

producer.description: Closes an open pull request without merging it. The pull request state is set to "closed" and it can be reopened later if needed. Use this action when you want to reject or abandon a pull request without merging the proposed changes into the base branch. You must have write access to the repository to close pull requests.

consumer.description: Removes a repository from a GitHub App installation for the authenticated user, given a valid `installation_id` and the `repository_id` of a repository currently linked to that installation; this operation is idempotent.

entries.notes: Closing a PR returns its base repository info (data.base.repo.id) -- a genuine, valid repository_id for that repo, reusable elsewhere even if the specific workflow (close a PR, then remove that repo from an app installation) is an unusual sequence. Data validity, not workflow plausibility, is the bar.

entries.label: team_slug

producer.description: Adds teams to the list of teams with push access to a protected branch. This action grants additional teams push access to a protected branch. Unlike 'Set team access restrictions' (PUT), this action adds to the existing list rather than replacing it entirely. Prerequisites: - The repository must be owned by an organization (not a personal account) - The branch must have protection rules enabled - The branch protection must have restrictions configured - The teams must exist in the organization and have repository access

consumer.description: Adds a GitHub user to a team or updates their role (member or maintainer), inviting them to the organization if not already a member; idempotent, returning current details if no change is made.

entries.notes: Producer requires teams (plural) as its own input -- you specify which teams to grant access to, and its response just confirms those same teams' slugs back. Circular in practice, but not caught by the circularity check, which only matches identical field names: 'teams' (plural, producer input) vs 'team_slug' (singular, the field being supplied) are literally different strings even though they refer to the same underlying data. A real, newly-found limitation: the circularity check misses plural/singular naming variations.

entries.label: secret_name

producer.description: Lists GitHub Actions secrets available for a specified organization.

consumer.description: Removes a repository's access to an organization-level Codespaces secret, if it was previously granted.

entries.notes: Producer explicitly lists GitHub Actions secrets (per its own description); consumer operates on an organization-level Codespaces secret -- same category mismatch as #22.

entries.label: userId

producer.description: Adds a GitHub user as a repository collaborator, or updates their permission if already a collaborator; `permission` applies to organization-owned repositories (personal ones default to 'push' and ignore this field), and an invitation may be created or permissions updated directly.

consumer.description: Tool to follow a GitHub user using GraphQL. Use when you need to make the authenticated user follow another user.

entries.notes: Same username-to-id lookup pattern as #7, for a different consumer.

entries.label: comment_number

producer.description: Lists all comments for a specific team discussion within an organization. Note: Team discussions are deprecated as of 2023-11-28. Consider using GitHub Discussions instead. This endpoint requires the authenticated user to be a member of the organization and have access to the team's discussions.

consumer.description: Lists reactions for a specific comment in a team discussion within an organization, optionally filtering by content type.

entries.notes: Both concern the same resource (team discussion comments) -- listing comments requires only discussion_number, comment_number is genuinely discovered from the list.

entries.label: comment_id

producer.description: Creates a new comment on an existing GitHub issue or pull request within the specified repository.

consumer.description: Lists reactions for a pull request review comment in a repository, optionally filtering by reaction type.

entries.notes: An issue comment id and a pull-request-review comment id are different, independently-numbered resources in the real GitHub API -- same class of cross-resource comment_id confusion as #19/#20.

entries.label: secret_name

producer.description: Lists all Codespaces secrets available for a specified organization, which must exist.

consumer.description: Creates or updates a Codespaces secret for the authenticated user; `encrypted_value` must be encrypted with the public key (ID: `key_id`) from GitHub's 'Get public key for the authenticated user' endpoint.

entries.notes: Producer lists ORGANIZATION Codespaces secrets; consumer creates/updates a Codespaces secret for the AUTHENTICATED USER (a personal secret). Org-scoped and user-scoped secrets are separate namespaces even within the same Codespaces category.

entries.label: pages_deployment_id

producer.description: Creates a GitHub Pages deployment for a repository using a specified artifact and OIDC token, provided GitHub Pages is enabled and the artifact (containing static assets) is accessible.

consumer.description: Retrieves the status of a specific GitHub Pages deployment for a repository, which must have GitHub Pages enabled.

entries.notes: pages_deployment_id is assigned by GitHub upon creating the deployment, genuinely new info.

entries.label: repository_id

producer.description: Closes an open pull request without merging it. The pull request state is set to "closed" and it can be reopened later if needed. Use this action when you want to reject or abandon a pull request without merging the proposed changes into the base branch. You must have write access to the repository to close pull requests.

consumer.description: Adds a repository to a GitHub App installation, granting the app access; requires authenticated user to have admin rights for the repository and access to the installation.

entries.notes: Same relationship as #24 (data.base.repo.id is a genuine, valid repository_id), different consumer tool.

entries.label: pull_number

producer.description: Primary tool to find and search pull requests. Supports filtering by repository, author, state, labels, and merge status, and returns structured PR data for reliable use in workflows. GitHub search results are capped at ~1000 total items; narrow filters when totals approach this limit. `created_since`/`updated_since` filter on creation/update timestamps, not `merged_at`; apply merge-date filtering client-side.

consumer.description: Adds reviewers to a specific pull request identified by owner, repo, and pull_number. This is NOT a search action - it operates on an already-known PR number. Requires `owner`, `repo`, `pull_number`, and at least one of `reviewers` or `team_reviewers`.

entries.notes: Searching for PRs requires no inputs and returns their pull_number -- the exact discover-then-act pattern the original README describes.

entries.label: deployment_id

producer.description: Enables a custom deployment protection rule for an existing environment in a repository by linking a configured GitHub App (via `integration_id`) to control deployments.

consumer.description: Lists all statuses for a given deployment in a repository.

entries.notes: The producer's response id identifies the newly-created protection RULE itself (a policy/configuration object), not any specific deployment instance -- a rule id and a deployment id are different resources that both happen to have a generic 'id' field.

entries.label: reaction_id

producer.description: Creates a reaction for a specified issue within a GitHub repository.

consumer.description: Deletes a reaction from a commit comment in a GitHub repository.

entries.notes: An issue reaction and a commit-comment reaction are separate, independently-numbered resources in GitHub's reactions API (scoped by target type). Consumer also requires comment_id, which creating an issue reaction has no way to supply.

entries.label: repository_names

producer.description: Creates a GitHub Codespace for the authenticated user, requiring a JSON request body with either `repository_id` (integer) or a `pull_request` object (containing `pull_request_number` (integer) and `repository_id` (integer)). This action allows users to set up a development environment quickly by creating a codespace from a specified repository or pull request.

consumer.description: Creates or updates values for an organization's predefined custom properties across multiple repositories (up to 30).

entries.notes: Consumer needs repository_names (plural, up to 30) but the producer only supplies a single repository's name from creating one codespace -- a singular value can't populate a plural/array-shaped field. Also inherits the same practical circularity as #1/#37 (a specific repo must already be known to create a codespace for it).

entries.label: codespace_name

producer.description: Creates a GitHub Codespace for the authenticated user, requiring a JSON request body with either `repository_id` (integer) or a `pull_request` object (containing `pull_request_number` (integer) and `repository_id` (integer)). This action allows users to set up a development environment quickly by creating a codespace from a specified repository or pull request.

consumer.description: Call to retrieve detailed information for a `codespace_name` belonging to the authenticated user, ensuring the codespace exists and is accessible.

entries.notes: The justifying field is CodespaceMachine.name -- the hardware/VM SKU name (e.g. 'standardLinux32gb'), not the codespace instance's own name. Coincidental match at the wrong nesting level of the schema: two unrelated 'name' fields under different parent types.

entries.label: pull_number

producer.description: Creates a new check run for a specific commit in a repository, used by external services to report status, detailed feedback, annotations, and images directly within the GitHub UI. NOTE: This endpoint requires GitHub App authentication - OAuth tokens and personal access tokens cannot create check runs.

consumer.description: Requests reviewers for a specific pull request identified by owner, repository, and pull request number. Use this action when you need to add individual users or teams as reviewers to an existing pull request. At least one of reviewers (individual users) or team_reviewers (teams) must be provided.

entries.notes: GitHub's real check-run API does include a pull_requests array identifying PRs associated with the checked commit -- a genuine, documented relationship, unlike #9's coincidental check-run/workflow-run token collision.

entries.label: user_login

producer.description: Adds assignees to a GitHub issue. This action only adds users - it does not remove existing assignees. Changes are silently ignored if the authenticated user lacks push access to the repository.

consumer.description: Tool to look up a pending enterprise administrator invitation by invitee, enterprise, and role. Use when you need to check if a specific user has a pending invitation to become an enterprise administrator.

entries.notes: user_login is a globally valid, context-independent GitHub username (unlike scoped resource IDs such as comment_id/secret_name/reaction_id, which only mean something within a specific sub-resource's namespace) -- it genuinely identifies the same person anywhere. The specific workflow (look up this particular assignee's enterprise invite status) is unusual, but per this project's own labeling criteria, data validity is the bar, not workflow plausibility.

entries.label: sponsorable_id

producer.description: Tool to list users and organizations who can be sponsored via GitHub Sponsors. Use when you need to discover sponsorable entities with optional filtering by dependency ecosystem.

consumer.description: Tool to create a new payment tier for your GitHub Sponsors profile using GraphQL. Use when you need to add a new sponsorship tier with a specific monthly price and description. The amount is specified in dollars and will be converted to cents automatically.

entries.notes: Listing sponsorable entities requires nothing; sponsorable_id is genuinely discovered from the list.

entries.label: thread_id

producer.description: Tool to list notification threads for the authenticated user with efficient polling support. Use when you need to fetch the user's GitHub notification inbox with filters like unread/participating/since. Returns notification threads plus polling headers (Last-Modified, ETag, X-Poll-Interval) for efficient polling. IMPORTANT: This endpoint requires a Personal Access Token (classic) with 'notifications' or 'repo' scope. It does NOT work with GitHub App tokens or fine-grained personal access tokens. If the token type is incompatible, a clear error message will be returned.

consumer.description: Marks an existing GitHub notification thread, identified by its `thread_id`, as read.

entries.notes: Listing notifications requires nothing; thread_id is genuinely discovered from the list.

entries.label: job_id

producer.description: Lists jobs for a specific workflow run in a GitHub repository.

consumer.description: Retrieves detailed information for a specific job within a GitHub Actions workflow run, given its `job_id` which must be valid for the specified repository's workflow.

entries.notes: Listing jobs for a workflow run requires only run_id; job_id is genuinely discovered from the list, both within the same workflow-run context.

entries.label: secret_name

producer.description: Lists the names and metadata (not values) of secrets for a specified, existing environment within an existing GitHub repository.

consumer.description: Replaces the list of repositories that can access an organization secret; only effective if the secret's visibility is 'selected'. To add or remove individual repositories without affecting others, use the dedicated add/remove repository actions instead.

entries.notes: Producer lists secrets scoped to a specific repository+environment; consumer operates on an organization-level secret. Environment-scoped and organization-scoped secret names are different namespaces, another instance of the recurring generic-identifier-spans-incompatible-scopes pattern.

consumer.description: Tool to get attestations by subject digest for a GitHub user. Use when you need to retrieve attestation data for a specific artifact or resource identified by its subject digest.

producer.description: Retrieves information for a GitHub Pages site, which must be enabled for the repository.

entries.label: value

producer.description: Retrieves detailed information about a specific issue in a repository using the owner, repository name, and issue number.

entries.label: username

entries.label: head_sha

entries.notes: An artifact's metadata includes the workflow_run that produced it, including its head_sha -- genuinely useful if you have an artifact and want to create a check run for the same commit it was built from.

entries.label: reviewers

producer.description: Creates a new environment or updates an existing one in a GitHub repository, allowing configuration of deployment protection rules such as wait timers and reviewers; ensure `environment_name` is URL-encoded if it contains special characters.

consumer.description: Removes currently assigned user logins and/or team slugs from a GitHub pull request's list of requested reviewers.

entries.notes: An environment's configured deployment-approval reviewers and a pull request's requested reviewers are different GitHub features (deployment protection vs PR review requests) that both happen to be called 'reviewers'. Also plausibly circular in practice: creating/updating an environment with protection rules typically means you specified the reviewers yourself as part of that same request.

entries.label: value_type

entries.notes: Listing an organization's existing custom properties reveals each one's value_type -- genuine discovery if you want to inspect or replicate an existing property's type.

consumer.description: Adds users to the list of people allowed to push to a protected branch in an organization repository. Important notes: - This action only works on organization-owned repositories (not personal repos) - The branch must already have protection rules with restrictions enabled - Users must have write access to the repository to be added - The combined total of users, apps, and teams is limited to 100 items

entries.notes: The data (a list of usernames currently restricted on this branch) is genuinely valid GitHub usernames, but re-adding users who are already on the restriction list isn't clearly new/useful information -- borderline between a real (if redundant) relationship and not representing genuine discovery. Labeled ambiguous rather than forcing a binary call.

entries.label: url_template

producer.description: Retrieves a specific autolink reference (which automatically hyperlinks text like 'JIRA-123' to an external system) for a repository using its unique ID; requires administrator access to the repository.

consumer.description: Creates a repository autolink to automatically convert text references (e.g., 'TICKET-123') into hyperlinks, using a unique `key_prefix` and a `url_template` that includes `<num>`.

entries.notes: url_template is user-authored configuration content (a URL pattern a human chooses when setting up an autolink), not system-assigned identifying data. Even though both fields share the same name/type, reusing one autolink's URL pattern to create an unrelated new autolink isn't discovering information you were missing -- it's an arbitrary content match, similar in spirit to the 'value' field case (#49) but for a more specific-sounding field name.

entries.label: branch

consumer.description: Tool to atomically create, update, or delete multiple files in a GitHub repository as a single commit. Uses Git Data APIs to avoid SHA mismatch conflicts that occur with the Contents API when multiple files are modified in parallel. Use when you need to make multi-file changes reliably. BRANCH CREATION: When committing to a new branch (e.g., 'fix/my-fix' or 'feature/new-feature'), you MUST provide 'base_branch' (typically 'main' or 'master') to create the branch from. If the branch already exists, base_branch is not needed. This action handles race conditions automatically: if the branch is updated by another commit between fetching the HEAD and updating the reference (resulting in a 422 'not a fast forward' error), the action will retry by refetching the HEAD and rebasing changes. Use max_retries to control this behavior.

entries.notes: Same reasoning as #45.

entries.label: devcontainer_path

producer.description: Creates a GitHub Codespace for the authenticated user, requiring a JSON request body with either `repository_id` (integer) or a `pull_request` object (containing `pull_request_number` (integer) and `repository_id` (integer)). This action allows users to set up a development environment quickly by creating a codespace from a specified repository or pull request.

consumer.description: Verifies if the authenticated user has accepted permissions for a specific devcontainer configuration in a repository, typically to ensure awareness before a codespace is created or used.

entries.notes: The devcontainer path is auto-detected by GitHub when creating the codespace -- genuinely new information you would not necessarily know in advance, independent of the separate circularity concern about needing to know which repository to create a codespace for.
